title: Continuous centimeter-level geodesy of the seismogenic seafloor

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a sustained observing system that tracks horizontal and vertical movement of the seafloor above major earthquake-generating subduction zones, at centimeter-level accuracy and with real-time delivery. It would make offshore deformation observable throughout the intervals between earthquakes and during shorter-lived changes, without depending on repeated ship measurement campaigns. The advance combines reliable three-dimensional measurements, temporal continuity and deployment at a scale useful for studying major megathrusts.

Its existing technical foundation is GNSS-Acoustic geodesy: surface-platform positions determined by satellite navigation are combined with acoustic measurements to seafloor transponder arrays. Converting acoustic travel times into positions requires information about sound speed through the water. Existing methods already recover useful seafloor positions and displacement histories; the proposed capability would extend this foundation to dependable continuous operation, especially for the less accurately measured vertical component.

significance.text: Offshore megathrust deformation is poorly constrained by land GNSS alone. Continuous seafloor observations would extend measurement into regions where land networks have limited resolving power, improving the spatial and temporal evidence available for studying subduction. Existing GNSS-A observations already capture interseismic, coseismic, postseismic and slow-slip deformation. The revolutionary potential lies in observing these processes with much greater continuity and geographic coverage, rather than discovering offshore deformation measurement for the first time.

The direct products would be positions, displacements and deformation histories. These could improve model-based estimates of plate-boundary coupling, locking, creep and slow slip, and help distinguish steady motion from transients that campaign sampling may resolve poorly. Those fault properties require interpretation and inversion: a seafloor network does not directly observe the buried fault interface or automatically identify where the next rupture will begin.

Conditional synthesis: the comparison with continuous land GPS is an analogy about the value of sustained observation, not an established equivalence in scientific impact. If reliable offshore deformation records became widely available, they could support better tests of earthquake-cycle models and eventually inform improved hazard assessments. Earthquake prediction would require additional advances and may remain unattainable; it is not a completion requirement or a consequence guaranteed by this innovation.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central gap is an integrated capability: continuous, real-time, centimeter-level three-dimensional observations across major megathrusts, with validated accuracy and operation independent of repeated ship measurement campaigns. Improving the precision of an individual campaign solution would address only part of this goal. The documented Japanese operational comparison lists GNSS-A observations approximately three to four times per year and horizontal uncertainty of 2–3 cm at one standard deviation. Moreover, formal uncertainties from an inversion can understate actual measurement errors.

Sound-speed estimation is a concrete obstacle because errors in the assumed water-column profile affect the inferred seafloor position, particularly its vertical component. Substituting an ocean analysis for in-situ profiles could reduce measurement effort, but agreement between two processing solutions does not independently establish either solution's absolute accuracy. A convincing system must demonstrate that its corrections remain adequate across changing ocean conditions and locations; the 2025 study also identifies uneven global HYCOM accuracy as a limitation.

Vertical errors must be assessed against the deformation being sought and the duration of observation. Centimeter-scale discrepancies can obscure small or short-lived signals, but they do not make all geodetic use impossible. The 2025 analysis reports that even a 10.3 cm vertical-position difference between Munk-profile and in-situ-profile solutions was associated with differences in overall displacement velocities only at the millimeter-per-year level. Persistent offsets, time-varying errors and long-term trends have different scientific consequences.

Engineering synthesis: sustained surface-platform operation, acoustic observations, position estimation and data delivery must function together for years, while installation and maintenance remain affordable. Operational reliability and deployment cost are therefore part of the breakthrough alongside measurement accuracy. Success at a few favorable sites would still leave questions about performance across different ocean environments and the resources required to maintain a much larger network.

current_state.text: A Japan Coast Guard poster reporting results through 2024 describes 27 sites in its SGO-A array and approximately 60 Japanese GNSS-A sites when university sites are included, compared with about 1,300 GEONET land stations. Its comparison lists continuous observations for land GNSS and approximately three to four observations per year for GNSS-A, with GNSS-A horizontal positioning uncertainty of 2–3 cm at one standard deviation. These are dated network counts and an operational baseline, rather than evidence for a general one-centimeter individual-transponder capability.

A document for the March 11, 2025 Japanese earthquake-research committee meeting covers observations from September 2012 through December 2024. For the Nemuro Peninsula offshore sites discussed, it reports lower accuracy in the vertical component than in the horizontal component and no significant vertical deformation obtained at that stage. This limitation is specific to those observations: the document discusses vertical tendencies elsewhere, so the Nemuro finding should not be generalized into an inability to measure vertical deformation at every site.

Tomita and Kido's 2024 report documents GNSS-A network extensions beyond Japan, including Taiwan, Cascadia and Alaska, and reviews measurements of interseismic, coseismic, postseismic and slow-slip deformation. Its discussion includes Cascadia results dating to 1998. The evidence therefore supports established international use, but does not justify describing every extension as a pilot or provide an inventory of worldwide continuous networks.

A Satellite Navigation study published June 30, 2025 reanalyzed campaign observations from four Japanese sites. When HYCOM sound-speed profiles replaced in-situ profiles, the resulting positions differed by 0.2 cm RMS horizontally and 2.9 cm RMS vertically; maximum differences were 1.8 cm and 9.1 cm, respectively. These numbers compare processing solutions using the in-situ-profile solution as a reference. They are not independently verified absolute positioning errors, and the experiment does not demonstrate continuous real-time operation or worldwide performance.

The supplied review had full article texts available for both journal studies, correcting the earlier research note's abstract-only description of the 2025 study. Its quantitative comparison is supported by article prose; the associated plots were not inspected. The dated evidence establishes useful regional geodesy and continuing observational limitations. Although the source copies were retrieved in November 2026, the supplied record contains no freshness search establishing whether subsequent developments have achieved the complete proposed capability anywhere worldwide.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate at least two major subduction-zone networks outside the existing Japanese arrays for several years, providing continuous horizontal and vertical positions at centimeter level with real-time delivery. Before deployment, define the accuracy statistic, reference frame, sampling interval, delivery latency, uptime and allowable drift. The choice of two zones and several years is a proposed test of transferability and sustained operation, not an established scientific standard.
completion_criteria.label: Multi-year centimeter-level real-time 3D positioning across two networks outside Japanese arrays

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: independently test sound-speed corrections and the resulting three-dimensional positions, including vertical performance, across the environmental conditions encountered. Demonstrate recovery of interseismic deformation and at least one transient, with uncertainty sufficient to distinguish the signal from measurement artifacts. Make the observations, corrections, uncertainty methods and analysis procedures available for independent reproduction. The assessment should distinguish absolute accuracy, repeatability and agreement between alternative processing solutions.
completion_criteria.label: Independently validated 3D positions resolve interseismic deformation and a transient

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: demonstrate sustained observations without repeated ship measurement campaigns, while documenting any maintenance or servicing that remains necessary. Report installation, maintenance and lifetime operating costs against an explicit affordability target. Passing these tests would establish demonstrated breadth across the tested regions and conditions. Wider readiness would require additional evidence about environmental variation, reliability and costs; two successful deployments cannot make every remaining megathrust installation a routine procurement exercise.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained observations without repeated ship measurements, with lifetime costs reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OCE-10, Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing, has the closest positioning overlap. OCE-08 concerns detecting very small movements of seafloor sites in a stable geodetic reference frame; OCE-10 concerns underwater positioning across a basin without surfacing. Acoustic navigation advances could serve both, but successful underwater navigation alone would not establish centimeter-level deformation accuracy or long-term vertical stability.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-02, Synoptic sensing of the ocean interior, overlaps through the need to characterize the water column, which could support sound-speed corrections. OCE-01, A closed theory of oceanic turbulent transport, is more indirectly related through understanding ocean variability. OCE-08 requires sufficiently accurate corrections for geodesy; it does not require either complete synoptic ocean sensing or a closed theory of turbulent transport, and would not establish those capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-04, Persistent mobile operations at full ocean depth, overlaps in sustained marine operation and the practical challenges of deployment and maintenance. Its defining goal is mobile full-depth operation, whereas OCE-08 centers on stable observations of seafloor deformation. OCE-05, Closure of ocean–crust fluid and biogeochemical exchange, shares the seafloor setting, but measures exchanges across the ocean–crust boundary rather than tectonic displacement. Neither entry is subsumed by a geodetic network.

Roster-based synthesis: the remaining concepts have more distant connections through ocean observation and modeling. OCE-03, A predictive closure of the biological carbon pump, and OCE-09, A predictive theory of pelagic size structure and trophic transfer, concern biological processes. OCE-06, A verified law of ice-shelf basal melting, and OCE-07, The stability class of the global overturning circulation, concern different physical systems and predictive questions. Shared infrastructure or environmental data could be useful, but demonstrating OCE-08 would not resolve those separate scientific goals.

change_log.change: Preserved OCE-08's identity and integrated its measurement principle, continuous-operation goal, vertical component and deployment scale into a standalone explanation.
change_log.reason: The innovation is a combined observing capability, rather than an incremental improvement to campaign positioning.

change_log.change: Replaced the general one-centimeter individual-transponder baseline with the documented 2–3 cm horizontal uncertainty at one standard deviation and approximately three to four annual GNSS-A observations.
change_log.reason: The operational comparison supports these figures, while the review warns that formal inversion uncertainty need not represent actual measurement error.

change_log.change: Replaced the blanket claim that centimeter-scale vertical errors disable scientific use with a distinction between transient detection and multiyear trend recovery.
change_log.reason: The 2025 study reports millimeter-per-year velocity differences despite a 10.3 cm vertical-position difference in one profile comparison.

change_log.change: Clarified that positions and deformation are observed directly, while locking, coupling, creep and slip require model-based interpretation.
change_log.reason: Land GNSS has limited offshore resolution rather than no sensitivity, and seafloor measurements do not directly reveal the buried fault or guarantee rupture-location identification.

change_log.change: Retained the conditional land-GPS analogy and potential scientific impact while separating them from earthquake prediction.
change_log.reason: The analogy is an impact judgment; prediction is neither demonstrated nor guaranteed by improved geodesy.

change_log.change: Preserved the Japanese network counts with their historical scope and restricted the Nemuro vertical limitation to the observations discussed.
change_log.reason: The counts describe results through 2024, and the committee document discusses vertical tendencies at other sites.

change_log.change: Removed the characterization of all international extensions as pilots.
change_log.reason: The 2024 report establishes use in Taiwan, Cascadia and Alaska, including older Cascadia results, without supporting that uniform characterization.

change_log.change: Expanded the HYCOM comparison to include four-site scope, RMS and maximum differences, and its reference-solution basis.
change_log.reason: The reported 0.2 cm horizontal and 2.9 cm vertical RMS differences are agreement between solutions, not independently established absolute accuracy.

change_log.change: Corrected the abstract-only access description and retained the limitation that the associated plots were not inspected in the supplied review.
change_log.reason: The supplied review reports full article texts and numerical support in prose; the final record should reflect that access without implying new inspection.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims about worldwide absence with a dated assessment and an explicit freshness gap.
change_log.reason: November 2026 retrieval does not establish that the 2024–2025 sources exhaust later developments.

change_log.change: Made completion criteria explicitly proposed and added measurable performance definitions, independent validation, reproducibility and lifetime costs.
change_log.reason: Centimeter-level accuracy, continuity, real-time delivery and affordability require operational definitions; two regional successes would not prove worldwide readiness.

change_log.change: Added roster-based overlap and distinction explanations without merging entries.
change_log.reason: The supplied roster supports conceptual comparisons but supplies no detailed evidence establishing dependencies among its innovations.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether the full continuous, real-time, centimeter-level three-dimensional capability remained unavailable worldwide as of November 2026.
The intended accuracy statistic, reference frame, sampling interval, latency, uptime and drift limits remain unspecified.
Independent absolute accuracy and geographic transferability are not established by the four-site HYCOM comparison; the adequate method and breadth of sound-speed validation remain to be defined.
No explicit affordability target or demonstrated installation, maintenance and lifetime operating costs are supplied.
The proposed transient-recovery test needs a defined signal scale and a way to assess performance if no suitable natural transient occurs during the deployment period.
The roster provides titles rather than detailed records for related concepts, so their overlaps are conceptual synthesis rather than verified technical dependencies.

brief.title: Continuous tracking of movement on the ocean floor
possible: Scientists could watch the ocean floor shift above major offshore earthquake faults, continuously and in real time. They could track sideways and up-and-down movement to centimeter-level accuracy for years, without repeated ship measurement trips.
why: Land instruments leave major gaps offshore. Continuous seafloor measurements would help researchers distinguish steady movement from brief changes and better estimate where buried faults stick or slip.
These records would let scientists test models of how faults behave between, during and after earthquakes. They could eventually improve earthquake hazard assessments for coastal communities.

sources.who: Japan Coast Guard’s seafloor deformation observation group
sources.showed: Its network has measured ongoing seafloor movement and slow slip, where faults move gradually. Its operational comparison describes occasional surveys rather than continuous observations.
sources.quote:
紀伊水道，熊野灘，足摺岬の沖合，豊後水道南方等多くの観測点で浅部長
期スロースリップによる変動が検出されている．
sources.cited_for: Seafloor measurements already reveal fault-related movement that land networks cannot fully capture.
sources.not_established: Occasional surveys do not establish continuous, real-time positioning with dependable vertical accuracy.

sources.who: Tohoku University and collaborating Japanese institutions
sources.showed: The team measured horizontal movement offshore of the Nemuro Peninsula. Less accurate vertical measurements did not reveal significant up-and-down movement there.
sources.quote:
上下成分については⽔平成分に⽐べて観測精度が低いため、現状で
は有意な変動は得られていない。
sources.cited_for: Vertical accuracy remains a practical obstacle at some sites.
sources.not_established: These observations do not establish reliable centimeter-level vertical tracking.

sources.showed: They built SeaGap, open software for calculating seafloor positions from satellite navigation and underwater sound measurements, and applied it to real observations.
sources.quote: Here, we developed a new GNSS-A positioning software, henceforth called “SeaGap” (Software of enhanced analyses for GNSS-acoustic positioning)
sources.cited_for: Positioning software and international seafloor observations provide an existing foundation.
sources.not_established: Software applied to observations does not establish a continuously operating offshore network.

sources.showed: At four Japanese sites, they recalculated seafloor positions using an ocean model instead of local sound-speed measurements. Long-term movement rates changed little.
sources.quote: the impact on displacement velocity is at the sub-mm/a level in the horizontal and mm/a level in the vertical.
sources.cited_for: Ocean models could reduce the effort needed to account for sound speed through seawater.
sources.not_established: Agreement between calculations does not establish absolute accuracy or reliable performance across different oceans.

shown: Japanese teams already measure seafloor movement between earthquakes, during them and afterward, including slow slip. Researchers also use these methods beyond Japan. They combine satellite navigation at the surface with sound signals sent to instruments on the seabed.
missing: Continuous, real-time centimeter-level tracking of both horizontal and vertical movement still needs a sustained demonstration across major offshore faults.
Independent tests must separate actual seabed movement from errors caused by changing sound speed through seawater.
Long-term operation without repeated ship measurements needs demonstrated reliability and affordable installation, servicing and lifetime costs.

milestones.label: Sustained, accurate tracking across two offshore networks
milestones.explanation: Networks in two major subduction zones, where plates sink beneath others, outside Japan’s existing arrays would have to deliver continuous centimeter-level positions in real time for years. This would test sustained operation across regions.

milestones.label: Independent checks distinguish steady movement and a brief change
milestones.explanation: Independent, reproducible checks would have to validate positions and sound-speed corrections, resolving movement between earthquakes and a brief change above measurement uncertainty. This would establish that the signals are real.

milestones.label: Sustained operation without repeated ship surveys at documented costs
milestones.explanation: Networks would have to operate without repeated ship measurements, document servicing, and report installation, maintenance and lifetime costs against an affordability target. This would test whether sustained observation is practical.

uncertain: The required accuracy measure, observation frequency, delivery delay, uptime and allowable drift still need clear definitions.
A brief-change test needs a defined signal size and a way to judge success if no suitable natural event occurs.
Better deformation records may improve hazard assessment, but they do not guarantee earthquake prediction.
